title: Working with coding assistants
subtitle: Practical guidance for planning, choosing a model, and checking an assistant's work.
sourceContext: This is an educational example specifically for Claude Code, not a ready-made system that works unchanged with every assistant. Useful patterns include criteria that fail until evidence is checked, a separate evaluator with fresh context, and progress notes for handing work to the next session. Its authors describe it as example ingredients from the Code with Claude event; adapt the ideas for other tools instead of copying the hooks blindly.

1.title: Define what done means
1.body: Write acceptance criteria before starting; leave each one incomplete until you inspect evidence.

2.title: Finish one step at a time
2.body: Keep each turn focused on one small, complete piece of work.

3.title: Check results with evidence
3.body: Inspect a real run, screenshot, or report instead of relying on the agent's claim.

4.title: Leave a handoff
4.body: Record changes, checks, and the next step so the next session can continue.

items.1: For a change across several files, write the goal and completion criteria first. Ask the assistant for a short plan and review it before implementation.
items.2: Use low reasoning for questions and small edits, medium for routine multi-file work, and high for difficult design or debugging. Higher levels can increase time and cost.
items.3: After a change, read the diff and test results. For work across sessions, record the current state, remaining tasks, and next step in a project file.

prompt: First summarize the goal and completion criteria. For multi-part work, propose a short plan and resolve open questions before implementation. Split the work into small steps; inspect real evidence for each criterion and do not mark it complete without evidence. At the end, record changes, tests, remaining work, and the next step in PROGRESS.md.
